question: Why do we measure a ship’s speed in knots?
headline: Sailors literally counted knots.
body: A weighted wooden board called a chip log was tossed overboard on a line tied with knots at even intervals. As the ship pulled away, a sailor counted how many knots slipped through his hands while a small sandglass ran out. That count was the speed, and the name stuck long after the rope was retired.

question: Why is the front panel of a car called the dashboard?
headline: It was built to block flying mud.
body: On horse-drawn carriages, the dashboard was a wooden or leather panel at the front that stopped mud and stones “dashed” up by the horses’ hooves from hitting the driver. Early cars kept a panel in the same spot, and the gauges ended up mounted on it.

question: Why is a cutoff time called a deadline?
headline: It was once a line you couldn’t cross alive.
body: In Civil War prison camps, most notoriously Andersonville in Georgia, the “dead line” was a boundary inside the stockade. Prisoners who crossed it could be shot by guards. By the 1920s, newspapers had borrowed the grim word for the cutoff time to file a story.

question: Why is sending out a radio or TV signal called broadcasting?
headline: It’s a farming word.
body: Before seed drills, farmers sowed by flinging seed in wide arcs by hand, which was called sowing “broadcast” — cast broadly. When radio began sending one signal out in every direction to anyone who cared to listen, the old farm word fit perfectly.

question: Why does “OK” mean all right?
headline: It started as a joke misspelling.
body: In 1830s Boston, newspapers had a fad for abbreviating deliberately misspelled phrases. “OK” stood for “oll korrect.” Most of those jokes faded, but OK got a huge boost in 1840 when supporters of President Martin Van Buren, nicknamed “Old Kinderhook,” formed OK Clubs.

question: Why is Bluetooth called Bluetooth?
headline: It’s named after a Viking king.
body: Harald “Bluetooth” Gormsson was a 10th-century king who brought together parts of Denmark and Norway. The engineers behind the standard liked the idea of one technology uniting different devices and borrowed his nickname. The logo is his initials, H and B, written in runes and merged.

question: Why is a hint that helps solve a mystery called a clue?
headline: A clue was a ball of thread.
body: The old spelling “clew” meant a ball of yarn. In the Greek myth, Theseus unspooled one to find his way back out of the Minotaur’s labyrinth. Anything that guides you through a puzzle became a clue.

question: Why is a bad dream called a nightmare?
headline: The “mare” isn’t a horse.
body: In Old English, a “mare” was a spirit believed to sit on sleepers’ chests and smother them. It’s an eerily good description of sleep paralysis, which can come with a crushing feeling of pressure and a sense of a presence in the room.

question: Why are muscles called muscles?
headline: Romans thought they looked like mice.
body: The Latin musculus means “little mouse.” A muscle flexing under the skin, especially in the upper arm, reminded people of a mouse scurrying beneath a cloth. The same Latin word also gave us “mussel,” for a similarly shaped shellfish.

question: Why is a window called a window?
headline: It’s an eye for the wind.
body: English borrowed it from Old Norse vindauga: vindr (wind) plus auga (eye). Early Scandinavian houses had an unglazed opening in the roof to let smoke out and air in. The Norse word pushed out the Old English one, which meant “eye-hole.”

question: Why are there 60 minutes in an hour?
headline: Thank the ancient Babylonians.
body: Babylonian mathematicians counted in base 60 rather than base 10. Sixty is handy because it divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30, which makes fractions easy. Later astronomers used their system to split hours and degrees into 60 parts, and we never switched.

question: Why does “checkmate” end a game of chess?
headline: It means “the king is helpless.”
body: Chess reached Europe from Persia by way of the Arabic-speaking world. The Persian shāh māt roughly means “the king is stuck” or “the king is defeated.” “Shah” also gave us “check,” and through the chequered board, “exchequer” and “cheque.”

question: Why are little-known facts called trivia?
headline: It’s where three roads meet.
body: The Latin trivium means a spot where three roads cross — a public place where people swapped small talk. In medieval schools, the trivium was also the three basic subjects: grammar, logic and rhetoric. Either way, the word came to mean ordinary, small things.

question: Why are jeans called jeans, and why is the fabric called denim?
headline: Both are named after cities.
body: Denim comes from the French serge de Nîmes, a sturdy cloth from the town of Nîmes in southern France. “Jeans” comes from Gênes, the French name for Genoa in Italy, where a tough cotton was made for sailors’ trousers.

question: Why do pilots call “Mayday” in an emergency?
headline: It’s French, sort of.
body: In 1923, a radio officer at London’s Croydon Airport, Frederick Mockford, was asked for a distress word everyone would recognize. Much of the traffic flew to and from Paris, so he picked “Mayday,” which sounds like the French m’aider — “help me.” It’s said three times so it can’t be mistaken.

question: Why is a catastrophe called a disaster?
headline: It means “bad star.”
body: From Italian disastro: dis- (bad) plus astro (star). When people believed the planets steered human fortunes, a calamity was literally an unfavorable alignment of the heavens. “Ill-starred” carries the same old idea.

question: Why are robots called robots?
headline: It’s the Czech word for forced labor.
body: In 1920, Karel Čapek wrote a play, R.U.R., about artificial workers who rebel against their makers. His brother Josef suggested calling them roboti, from robota — drudgery, the unpaid work serfs owed their lords. The play was a hit and the word went global.

question: What does Wi-Fi stand for?
headline: Nothing at all.
body: In 1999, the branding firm Interbrand coined Wi-Fi as a catchier name than “IEEE 802.11b Direct Sequence,” playing on “hi-fi.” The “wireless fidelity” explanation was tacked on later, and the industry group behind it has since said the name doesn’t stand for anything.

question: Why is a friend you spend time with called a companion?
headline: It’s someone you share bread with.
body: From Latin com- (with) plus panis (bread). A companion was literally someone you broke bread with. “Company” comes from the same root, and so do Spanish compañero and French copain.

question: Why does cutting an onion make you cry?
headline: You’re setting off a tiny chemical weapon.
body: Slicing an onion breaks its cells, mixing chemicals that are normally kept apart. They react to form a gas called syn-propanethial-S-oxide, which drifts up and irritates the nerves in your eyes, so they flood with tears to wash it away. It likely evolved to stop animals from eating the bulb.

question: What’s the tiny pocket on your jeans for?
headline: A pocket watch.
body: When Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented riveted work pants in 1873, the small front pocket was there to keep a pocket watch safe and handy. Wristwatches took over decades later, but the pocket stayed. Today it mostly holds coins, keys, or nothing at all.

question: Why do airplane windows have rounded corners?
headline: Square ones helped tear planes apart.
body: The first jet airliner, the de Havilland Comet, suffered fatal breakups in 1954. Investigators found metal fatigue: repeated pressurizing at altitude concentrated stress at sharp corners in the fuselage until cracks spread. Rounded openings spread that stress out, and every airliner since has used them.

question: Why do we say goodbye?
headline: It’s a squashed-down blessing.
body: In the 1500s, people parted by saying “God be with ye.” Through constant use it shrank to something like “godbwye.” Influenced by phrases like “good day” and “good night,” the “God” slowly turned into “good.”

question: Why is a home loan called a mortgage?
headline: It’s a “death pledge.”
body: From Old French mort (dead) plus gage (pledge). Old legal writers explained that the pledge “dies” one of two ways: when the debt is paid off, or when the borrower fails to pay and the property is lost.

question: Why are independent workers called freelancers?
headline: They were literally free lances.
body: Sir Walter Scott’s 1819 novel Ivanhoe described medieval knights for hire as “free lances” — fighters not sworn to any one lord. By the late 1800s the term was used for politicians without a party, and soon after for writers and workers without a fixed employer.

question: Why is a clock called a clock?
headline: A clock was originally a bell.
body: Early mechanical clocks in medieval monasteries and towers often had no face; they rang bells to mark the hours of prayer. The word traces back to medieval Latin clocca, “bell,” a cousin of French cloche and German Glocke.

question: Why is a daisy called a daisy?
headline: It’s the day’s eye.
body: Old English dægesēage means “day’s eye.” The flower opens its petals at dawn to reveal its yellow center and closes them at dusk, like an eye waking up and going to sleep.

question: Why is junk email called spam?
headline: Blame Monty Python.
body: In a 1970 sketch, a café serves Spam with nearly everything while a group of Vikings drowns out all conversation by chanting “Spam, Spam, Spam.” Early internet users borrowed the joke for floods of repetitive junk that drown out real messages.

question: Why are computer glitches called bugs?
headline: The famous moth was already a joke.
body: In 1947, operators of the Harvard Mark II found a moth trapped in a relay and taped it into the logbook as the “first actual case of bug being found.” It was funny because engineers had been calling glitches “bugs” since at least Thomas Edison in the 1870s.

question: Why is “pound” abbreviated lb?
headline: It’s Latin.
body: The Roman unit of weight was the libra, from the word for scales. “Pound” comes from the Latin phrase libra pondo, “a pound by weight.” English kept “pound” from one half and the abbreviation lb from the other — and the £ sign is a fancy L for libra too.
